questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of n items?
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — each comparison halves the search space, so at most log₂(n) steps are needed.
questions.feedbackWrong: Binary search discards half the remaining items every step — halving behaviour is logarithmic, O(log n).

mistakes.misconception: Confuses binary search with linear search.
mistakes.correction: Linear search checks each item once — O(n). Binary search exploits the sorted order to skip half the data each step.

questions.prompt: List the steps of one pass of a bubble sort on the array [5, 2, 8, 1], showing the array after each comparison/swap decision.

markScheme.text: Compares 5 and 8, no swap; then 8 and 1, swaps: [2, 5, 1, 8].
Pass ends with 8 in final position — largest element has 'bubbled' to the end.

questions.prompt: For large inputs, which sorting algorithm is fastest in the worst case?
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — merge sort is O(n log n) in all cases; quick sort degrades to O(n²) in the worst case and bubble/insertion are O(n²).
questions.feedbackWrong: Compare worst cases: bubble, insertion and quick sort are all O(n²) worst-case — merge sort guarantees O(n log n).

mistakes.misconception: Knows quick sort is fastest in practice on average.
mistakes.correction: Average-case quick sort is fast, but its worst case is O(n²) — the question asks worst case, where merge sort wins.

questions.prompt: Describe the role of the Program Counter (PC), Memory Address Register (MAR), Memory Data Register (MDR) and Accumulator during the fetch stage of the fetch-decode-execute cycle.

markScheme.text: PC holds the address of the next instruction to fetch.
PC contents copied to MAR; the MAR carries the address to memory.
Instruction at that address is transferred into the MDR (and then CIR).
Accumulator's role is in execution: it stores results of ALU operations — not part of the fetch itself.

questions.prompt: Why does adding cache memory speed up a computer?
options: Cache is faster memory close to the CPU, storing frequently-used instructions
Cache increases the clock speed of the processor
Cache stores files permanently so the disk is never needed
Cache adds extra cores for parallel processing
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — cache is fast SRAM on or near the CPU; frequently-needed data avoids slow main-memory access.
questions.feedbackWrong: Cache is small fast memory between CPU and RAM — it works because programs reuse the same data (locality), so fewer slow memory fetches occur.

mistakes.correction: Cache is volatile working memory, not file storage — it holds copies of data that also lives in RAM.

questions.prompt:
Trace this insertion-sort inner loop on a = [4, 3].
```
j = 0
key = a[1]
while j >= 0 and a[j] > key
  a[j+1] = a[j]
  j = j - 1
endwhile
a[j+1] = key
```
questions.guidance: Record the initial values first, then one row per loop iteration showing j, key and the array after that iteration completes, and finally a row after the loop-exit assignment.

questions.prompt: State one difference between Von Neumann and Harvard architecture and one consequence of that difference.

markScheme.text: Von Neumann stores instructions and data in the same memory/bus; Harvard uses separate memories/buses.
Consequence: Harvard can fetch instruction and data simultaneously (faster); Von Neumann suffers the bottleneck but is simpler/cheaper.

questions.prompt: Which data structure is essential for breadth-first graph traversal?
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — BFS explores level by level using a FIFO queue; DFS uses a stack.
questions.feedbackWrong: BFS visits nodes in order of discovery — first in, first out — which is exactly queue behaviour.

mistakes.correction: Depth-first search plunges deep using a stack (LIFO); breadth-first spreads evenly using a queue (FIFO).
